comments.author: @1kzrider
comments.text:
That final part about a salary reset couldn't be more spot-on. When I was working my last IT position—by the blessings of the Lord, our Savior—my finances were not terrible. My wife and I shop at thrift stores, drive used cars, and rarely eat out. That wasn't just due to cash, either.

The thing is, if you're not in debt and have some savings, you can be jobless for at least six months—and that puts you in control. When you're not afraid to speak up, they hate it. I had enough savings to hold me over for more than a year, which made me a total threat. They tried to push me out using every tactic in the book, so I waited for the right moment: when another team member was quitting.

Our team had already been reduced from seven staff members down to four, leaving three of us severely overloaded. To make matters worse, one member who got promoted over us was extremely lazy—we were constantly propping up his work. Yet, he was the one who got promoted! So, I quit the very same day. That left them with just one lazy staff member who also missed work weekly. I left them high and dry. MIC DROP. It never felt so good.

Employers hate an employee who isn't a "yes, YES, YES, I will do whatever you say" person. Anyone who can say no—and prove why an idea is bad using facts—becomes an immediate target. Anyone who complains about being understaffed becomes a target. Anyone who isn't willing to put in 10 unpaid hours a week becomes a target.

I also figured out that the whole one-hour lunch rule is a scam. A company telling you, "We take a one-hour lunch here," is doing it for them, not for you. When you're short on pay, you sit at your desk and eat a dry, two-day-old sandwich—and they know you'll just keep working through that hour while eating food brought from home. I watched this happen at several companies while upper management left daily, laughing and joking on their way to eat at restaurants.
